title: AI prediction leads people to forgo guaranteed rewards
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the mere presence of AI prediction can change how people make decisions, beyond simply providing information or recommendations. The authors focus on a Newcomb’s paradox-inspired choice task in which participants must decide between taking a guaranteed reward and choosing a higher-risk option whose payoff has supposedly already been determined by a prediction about their behavior.

Across four preregistered online experiments, participants were assigned to AI-prediction, human-expert prediction, random-control, or no-prediction conditions. In the core task, people chose between opening both boxes for a guaranteed smaller gain or only the predicted box for a potentially larger payoff. Additional studies varied interaction style, generalized the effect to vignette scenarios, and tested repeated exposure over five rounds. Some AI conditions used an LLM-based chatbot (OpenAI GPT-4.1) to increase the sense of interaction, while other conditions used only the label or icon of an AI predictor.

The studies were run with 1,305 adult online participants recruited through Prolific in the United States. Results showed that framing the decision as predicted by AI substantially increased one-boxing, meaning more participants forwent the guaranteed reward. The effect generalized across contexts and persisted even after repeated predictive failures. The authors conclude that perceived predictive authority can reshape decision-making through a mechanism they call predictive binding, where people align their actions with what they think an AI “knows” they will do.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a preregistered multi-study experimental paper with randomized conditions and a fairly large combined sample (N=1,305), but it is not an education study and does not evaluate a K-12 intervention or learner outcome. The evidence is rigorous for the behavioral question it asks, yet only indirectly relevant to education research and not an RCT of an educational technology.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no K-12 academic, scientific reasoning, or educational implementation outcomes. Its findings are about adult decision-making under AI prediction framing, so it has no demonstrated impact on science learning or schooling outcomes.

interventions.use_case: AI prediction framed as a predictive authority in a Newcomb-paradox-style decision task, including an LLM-based chatbot interaction in one condition and AI-labeled prediction in repeated-choice experiments
